key: D minor → D major (written score; playback pitch unverified)
performers: Marian Anderson, contralto; San Francisco Symphony Orchestra; Pierre Monteux, conductor
intro: Marian Anderson sings “In diesem Wetter, in diesem Braus”, the storm song and lullaby that end Kindertotenlieder, with Pierre Monteux and the San Francisco Symphony. After the parent’s repeated protest, the song turns to a lullaby of shelter, accompanied by celesta and rocking strings.

cues.title: Opening, harp and cello tremolos
cues.text: The harp plays sharp accents while flutes and clarinets pass short phrases over the muted strings, with the cellos in tremolo beneath. Mahler marked the opening Mit ruhelos schmerzvollem Ausdruck (with restless, painful expression). Anderson’s part is set above this texture.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460 (1905), p. 60: Mit ruhelos schmerzvollem Ausdruck, muted strings, cello tremolos and harp accents. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Opening march in D minor
cues.text: The song opens with a march in D minor, the only song in the cycle to do so. Its key and melodic style recall the first movement of Mahler’s Third Symphony, written in 1895–96.
cues.evidence: Reinhold Kubik, Universal Edition introduction to Kindertotenlieder (autumn 2008): song 5 “is the only song to open with a Mahler-style march”, recalling the key and melodic style of the Third Symphony’s first movement (song bar 9, symphony bar 136): https://www.universaledition.com/en/Kindertotenlieder/P0045027

cues.title: The fears that come too late
cues.text: Rückert’s parent worries that the children might fall ill, then that they might die tomorrow. Each fear collapses as soon as it is spoken. “Das sind nun eitle Gedanken” — those are idle thoughts now. The children have already been carried away.
cues.evidence: Rückert, In diesem Wetter, second and third stanzas; German text at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kindertotenlieder#Text. Our translation.

cues.title: Scoring of the fifth song
cues.text: Only this last song calls for a piccolo, a contrabassoon and a third and fourth horn. The cycle has no trumpets or trombones.
cues.evidence: Mahler catalogue, Kindertotenlieder, scoring list: piccolo and contrabassoon in no. 5 only, horns 3–4 in no. 5 only: https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/KtL/KtL.htm The Mahler Foundation confirms there are no trumpets: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/kindertotenlieder/kindertotenlieder-introduction/

cues.title: Rehearsal 8, piccolo and Glöckchen
cues.text: At rehearsal 8 the piccolo holds a high note above the orchestra, and a small bell (Glöckchen) sounds in the gaps. Under the marking Allmählich langsamer, the string phrases become slower and shorter. This bridge leads from the storm music into Anderson’s final stanza.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 78–79: rehearsal 8, piccolo, Glöckchen and Allmählich langsamer.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final stanza, “Wie ein Wiegenlied”
cues.text: Mahler marks the final stanza “Wie ein Wiegenlied” — like a lullaby. Anderson repeats the weather words of the opening over celesta and rocking strings. In Rückert’s text the children now rest as safely as in their mother’s house, “von Gottes Hand bedecket” — covered by God’s hand.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 79–84: Mahler’s marking and Rückert’s last stanza; our translations. The score moves from D minor to D major; this transfer’s playback pitch is unverified.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mahler to Guido Adler, 1907
cues.text: Mahler finished the cycle in 1904. In July 1907 his elder daughter, Maria, died of scarlet fever and diphtheria. He told Guido Adler that he had imagined “a child of mine had died”, and that after truly losing a daughter he “could not have written these songs any more.”
cues.evidence: Mahler to Guido Adler after Maria’s death in 1907, as quoted by Theodor Reik, The Haunting Melody (1953), p. 315, and repeated in Peter Russell, Light in Battle with Darkness: Mahler’s Kindertotenlieder (1991) and on the Mahler Foundation’s introduction: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/kindertotenlieder/kindertotenlieder-introduction/ (Reik and Russell seen only as full-text excerpts; the letter itself has not been traced). Maria’s death on 11 July 1907: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/the-man/health/ Kubik places the songs in the summers of 1901 and 1904: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Kindertotenlieder/P0045027

cues.title: Orchestral postlude
cues.text: The violas continue the cradle rhythm after Anderson’s last words. Bassoon and horns play softly over divided cellos, and the celesta has the short descending figures of the last page. The final chord fades, Morendo, under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 84–86, rehearsal 10 and the closing page: weich, Morendo dim. and the final fermata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Performance instruction in the score, 1905
cues.text: In a footnote on the first page of the score, Mahler described the five songs as “ein einheitliches, untrennbares Ganzes” — one unified, inseparable whole. He asked that their continuity be preserved, including through the pauses between songs, and that there be no applause.
cues.evidence: Mahler’s performance instruction, C. F. Kahnt full score (1905), p. 3, footnote; our translation. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425

cues.title: Cello allusion to the Third Symphony
cues.text: In the last five bars (bars 129–133) a cello melody alludes to the first theme of the Third Symphony’s finale, a movement titled “What love tells me”. The musicologist Andreas Dorschel took the allusion to state the cycle’s conclusion, “that death is powerful, yet love is even stronger.”
cues.evidence: Andreas Dorschel, “Trost für die Untröstlichen. Mahlers Kindertotenlieder und Bergs Violinkonzert”, Musikfreunde 25 (2012/13), no. 5, pp. 34–37 (article not opened; the allusion, mm. 129–133 of song 5, and the quoted sentence as given on the Mahler Foundation’s introduction): https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/kindertotenlieder/kindertotenlieder-introduction/ Kahnt full score, p. 86: the cellos’ pp morendo phrase in the last bars: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425

transitions.title: The piccolo holds above the bell
transitions.from: A · Short wind phrases over cellos
transitions.how: The piccolo holds a note, written D, above repeated taps on the small bell. Harp chords and low bassoon notes continue below. Under Allmählich langsamer (gradually slower), the strings play falling figures that grow smaller with each wave, and the lullaby follows. The passage comes at rehearsal 8 of the Kahnt full score, pp. 78–79.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 78–79, rehearsal 8. The held note is written D; the transfer’s playback pitch is unverified. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425

transitions.title: Celesta entry at the lullaby
transitions.how: The piccolo holds across the change from D minor to D major. At Langsam. Wie ein Wiegenlied, the celesta joins the rocking strings, and the low strings rest beneath Anderson’s quiet return. The melody keeps the opening words about the weather.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 79: D minor to D major, celesta entry and lullaby marking. Key names describe the score; the recording’s playback pitch is unverified.

transitions.title: Horns take over the lullaby
transitions.to: Coda · bassoon and horns after the voice
transitions.how: Anderson’s last “Haus” ends while the violas continue their rocking figure. Divided cellos sustain beneath them. Horn and bassoon enter with soft phrases marked weich and carry the major-key lullaby into the instrumental ending without a break.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 84–86, rehearsal 10 and the D-major ending. Key names describe the score; the recording’s playback pitch is unverified.

source.title: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, full score (C. F. Kahnt, plate 4460)
source.locator: Song V, printed pp. 60–86: storm music, the high piccolo and small bell, then the lullaby with celesta.

timeline.note: Opening storm: short wind figures, muted strings, tremolo cellos and accented harp chords.
Anderson’s line cuts across the short wind phrases and the moving string figures.
A held high piccolo note and the small bell remain as the storm subsides.
Celesta and soft strings accompany the lullaby; the bass line falls silent at its opening.
Horn and bassoon continue after the voice, with rocking violas and divided cellos.
The celesta descends while winds and strings hold the final chord.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor.
